A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KPE/KTS research. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching the original Appendix G/H visualizations to Appendix J/K in v2.

before.justification: Sections 4–6 report original synthetic-data and image-generation experiments, including KPE correlations, training dynamics, and KTS quality and memorization results.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds representation, numerical stability, schedule sensitivity and noise-injection comparisons.

M1.justification: The KPE definition and proposed KTS procedure remain unchanged: velocity rescaling with linear early launch, exponential late damping, default phase boundary 0.6 and k=3. Alternative schedules are tested as ablations; they do not replace the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same three synthetic distributions, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-256 and CelebA experiments. New analyses reuse this coverage. Appendix F corrects 'four' synthetic datasets to 'three'; both versions actually describe and evaluate the same three.

E2.justification: Appendix I.4 and Table 11 add inference-time Gaussian velocity-noise injection at sigma=0.005 and 0.01 as comparators against FM and KTS on CelebA. Existing neural-versus-empirical FM and FM-versus-KTS comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include a 4,000-sample feature-space comparison, phase-boundary and schedule grids, solver/NFE/time-grid comparisons, neighborhood-size sweeps, and reintegration of 200 matched noise vectors. Section 5.3 also changes the stated midpoint budget from 100 steps to NFE=100; this establishes a reported setting revision, without establishing that the retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the original alpha/beta ablations. Table 3 tests representation dependence; Tables 6–8 test phase boundaries, schedule functions and numerical settings; Appendices G/H test KPE ranking stability and neighborhood-size sensitivity. Table 11 tests whether generic noise perturbations reproduce KTS benefits.

E5.justification: Appendix G newly specifies seed 42 for the shared bank of 200 initial noise vectors. Existing mean/standard-deviation reporting, Bonferroni-corrected tests and effect sizes remain unchanged. No increased independent-run count or new confidence-interval reporting is established.

E6.justification: Original numerical Tables 1–4 are retained as v2 Tables 1, 2, 4 and 5. Tables 3 and 6–11 add substantial results, including minimum cross-configuration KPE rank correlation 0.9921. Table 11 reports noise injection at sigma=0.005 achieving FID 17.48 and memorization 35.31%, versus KTS 14.35 and 31.22%. These are added comparisons, not improvements over v1's matched KTS scores.

T1.justification: Appendix I adds a spatial Lipschitz assumption and a proved Gronwall stability bound for KTS trajectory displacement. Appendix B makes nondegeneracy assumptions explicit and restricts the integrated energy bound to interior intervals under posterior dominance. Appendix D removes the additional divergence claim and argument following the terminal-gap lower bound. These materially extend and revise the theory.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion narrow the second headline finding from data-manifold rarity to local sparsity in representation space; the introduction explicitly identifies the theoretical density as that of the bridge mixture. The semantic-fidelity, memorization and KTS contributions remain.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 replaces the assertion that exact matching requires a terminal impulse with a conditional explanation based on how quickly the terminal gap closes. Section 6 and Appendix I add explanations of time-conditioned velocity rescaling, bounded perturbations and limited distributional change, using retained precision/recall results. New robustness and noise controls support additional interpretations of KTS's phase structure.

D1.justification: Section 6.2 newly spells out the nearest/second-nearest pixel-space gap ratio and the 10,000-sample memorization evaluation. Additional experiments document feature dimensions, checkpoint selection, noise controls and perturbation strengths. These expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the retained training architecture or hyperparameters.

R1.justification: v2 adds Lim (2025), 'On the hidden biases of flow matching samplers,' in Section 4.3 and Appendix A. Appendix C explicitly acknowledges the analogous derivation in Bertrand et al. (2025), already cited in v1. The broader research positioning remains.

P1.justification: v2 edits terminology, headings, explanatory paragraphs and notation, updates author/venue information and acknowledgements, and reorganizes some appendix introductions. The main section sequence and narrative remain recognizable; the largest expansions primarily document new scientific analyses.

P2.justification: Seven new numbered tables substantially expand the displayed evidence, including sensitivity comparisons and a solver-correlation matrix. Existing tables and Algorithm 1 are repositioned, and the visualization appendices move to J/K. Several retained figures are downsampled or rasterized, reducing fine-label clarity without adding new visual results.

improvement.justification: Tables 3 and 6–11 address important weaknesses in v1's evidence concerning representation choice, discretization, KTS schedules and generic perturbation alternatives. Together with narrower claims, revised Appendix B/D reasoning and the new stability proof, these substantially strengthen support for KPE and KTS. The full-trajectory assertion in Remark 4.3 remains inconsistent with the restricted Appendix B.4.2 bound, and some figures lose clarity, but these limitations do not outweigh the validation gains.
